title-group.article-title: Fetal spina bifida associates with dysregulation in nutrient‐sensitive placental gene networks: Findings from a matched case–control study

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: To improve outcomes in fetuses with spina bifida (SB), better understanding is needed of the molecular drivers of SB and its comorbidities. Pregnant people carrying a fetus with isolated SB (cases; n = 12) or a fetus with no congenital anomalies (controls; n = 21) were recruited at Mount Sinai Hospital, Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Clinical data and placental samples were collected. Placental transcriptome was sequenced (Clariom D microarray) and a nutrient‐focused gene expression analysis pipeline was applied to determine whether fetal SB associates with placental dysfunction. Of the 391 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in cases, 11% (n = 42) had at least one nutrient cofactor, including B vitamins (n = 7 genes), iron/heme (n = 6), and zinc (n = 11). Cases had dysregulation in genes not previously known to associate with SB, and in placental genes that have known links to SB but have not been previously identified in the placenta. Cases also had downregulated nutrient transport and upregulated branching angiogenesis and immune/inflammatory processes. Five nutrient‐dependent transcription regulators, collectively predicted to target 46% of DEGs in cases, were identified and were most commonly dependent on B vitamins (n = 3) and zinc (n = 2). Placental gene expression changes were most acute in cases with poor growth. Placentae from fetuses with SB have dysregulation in several gene networks, including those that are sensitive to multiple micronutrients beyond the well‐known folic acid. An improved understanding of placental phenotype in fetuses with SB may help identify novel mechanisms associated with comorbidities in fetuses with SB, and reveal new targets to improve fetal outcomes in this population.

p.bold: WHAT IS THE CURRENT KNOWLEDGE ON THE TOPIC?

boxed-text.p:
Spina bifida (SB) can associate with reduced fetal growth. However, little is known about placental development and function in pregnancies with fetal SB, despite that the placenta is a critical regulator of fetal growth.
WHAT QUESTION DID THIS STUDY ADDRESS?

How is placental gene expression altered in fetuses with SB? Is dysregulation in placental genes and networks evident in gene sets that are nutrient‐sensitive, or those critical for fetoplacental growth?
WHAT DOES THIS STUDY ADD TO OUR KNOWLEDGE?

Fetuses with SB have dysregulation in placental genes not previously known to associate with SB, and in placental genes that have known links to SB but have not been previously identified in the placenta. Fundamental placental processes are also dysregulated in fetuses with SB, including gene sets involved in placental nutrient transport, branching angiogenesis, and immune/inflammatory processes. Several dysregulated placental genes and gene regulatory networks in fetuses with SB are sensitive to multiple micronutrients, emphasizing the need to expand beyond a folic acid‐centric view to understand SB and its comorbidities. This study is the first to assess global placental gene expression in fetuses with SB and the first to use a novel nutrient‐focused gene expression analysis pipeline in gestational tissues. It is also among the first to interrogate placental phenotype in fetuses with SB more broadly.
HOW MIGHT THIS CHANGE CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY OR TRANSLATIONAL SCIENCE?

An improved understanding of placental phenotype in fetuses with SB may help identify novel mechanisms associated with comorbidities in fetuses with SB and reveal new therapeutic targets to improve fetal outcomes in this population.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Risk factors for neural tube defects (NTDs) include nutritional factors, 1 genetic susceptibilities, and immune and metabolic dysregulation, 2 , 3 yet only ~50% of NTDs are prevented by current public health approaches. 4 This may be in part because the primary approach to reduce NTD incidence, improving maternal periconceptional folate status, only focuses on one potential mechanism. An improved understanding of other drivers of NTDs, and of how multiple risk factors may co‐occur to increase the risk of NTDs, could help prevent the over 300,000 NTDs that affect newborns globally each year, and reduce morbidity risk in children with NTDs. 5

The risk factors known to associate with NTDs are likely to also disrupt proper placental growth and development, which may in part explain why fetuses with NTDs have an increased risk of growth restriction and early birth. 6 , 7 , 8 Optimal placentation, beginning during the first week post‐fertilization and continuing across pregnancy, relies on proper immune signaling and cells 9 and bioavailable nutrients. 10 Thus, an early pregnancy environment permissive of NTDs may also associate with placental maldevelopment and dysfunction, which could drive comorbidities in fetuses with NTDs. 6 , 7 , 8 We have previously shown in a historical cohort that fetuses with NTDs have an increased risk of altered placental structure/pathology. 7 However, a more comprehensive analysis of placental function in pregnancies with fetal NTDs may reveal insights into functional contributors to comorbidities in these pregnancies, and novel gene signatures associated with NTDs.

To better understand how placental function is altered in fetuses with NTDs, we used data from a case–control study to determine how the placental transcriptome differs in fetuses with isolated spina bifida (SB; the most common NTD; cases), compared to fetuses without any congenital anomalies (controls). We hypothesized that placental transcriptome profiles in cases would be distinct from controls, especially in cases with poorer growth outcomes, and that dysregulation would be evident in gene sets critical for fetoplacental growth. We also hypothesized that multiple nutrient‐sensitive gene networks would be dysregulated in cases.

sec.title: METHODS
sec.p: Additional details are provided in the Supplementary Methods S1.

sec.title: Ethics
sec.p: This study was approved by the Carleton University Research Ethics Board (108884 and 106932) and the Mount Sinai Hospital Research Ethics Board (17‐0028‐E and 17‐0186‐E).

sec.title: Population and study design
sec.p: Pregnant people carrying a fetus with open SB (cases) were prospectively recruited in a case–control study from the Fetal Medicine Unit at Mount Sinai Hospital, Toronto, Canada, in the early third trimester of pregnancy. Fetuses with structural anomalies outside the SB spectrum and those with genetic anomalies were excluded. Pregnant people carrying a fetus without congenital anomalies were recruited from our low‐risk pregnancy unit (controls) around 25 weeks' gestation. Placentae were collected from 12 cases and 10 controls. Because the controls were all born full term, a second control group was identified to match to cases based on gestational age (GA) at delivery. These controls delivered preterm (PT; hereafter PT controls; n = 12) but had no other known pregnancy complications. PT controls were matched 1:1 with cases for GA at delivery and maternal pre‐pregnancy body mass index classification. Thus, we had two groups against which the cases were compared: controls (born full term) and PT controls.

sec.title: Maternal clinical, demographic, and dietary characteristics
Infant birth outcomes
Sample collection
sec.p: Placental biopsies were collected and processed by the Research Centre for Women's and Infants' Health immediately after delivery. Placental samples were collected from each placental quadrant and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C until further processing. 13

sec.title: RNA extraction and expression profiling
sec.p: RNA was extracted from whole placental homogenates using the Qiagen RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen, Toronto, Canada) and RNA quality control and microarray sequencing were carried out by Genome Québec (Montreal, Canada; Table S1). Placental transcriptome profiles were determined using the Clariom D microarray (human) and the GeneChip WT Pico Kit.

sec.title: Gene‐level transcriptome analysis
sec.p: Raw expression files were processed in Transcription Analysis Console software (version 4.0.2). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) from cases compared to PT controls, and cases compared to controls were identified using the eBayes method (Benjamini‐Hochberg q value <0.05; absolute log fold change [FC] ≥ 2). 14 , 15 , 16 The overlap between the two DEG lists (i.e., genes that were differentially expressed both in cases compared to PT controls and in cases compared to controls) was identified and carried forward in subsequent analyses.

Functional analysis of DEGs was performed using Gene Ontology terms and the Protein ANalysis THrough Evolutionary Relationships (PANTHER) classification system (version 16.0). 17 DEGs with known cell‐specific expression at the maternal‐fetal interface were also identified (expression threshold ≥1; PlacentaCellEnrich) and characterized according to known expression patterns in the placenta. 18 DEGs that coded for micronutrient‐dependent proteins (i.e., proteins with ≥1 micronutrient cofactor) were identified and used to construct DEG‐nutrient interaction networks. 19 , 20

sec.title: Pathway‐level transcriptome analysis
sec.p: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA; version 4.2.3) was used to identify upregulated and downregulated gene sets in cases compared to PT controls and controls, following recommended methods. 21 Gene sets upregulated or downregulated in cases compared to both PT controls and controls (q < 0.05) were identified and carried forward for interpretations and visualizations.

sec.title: Network‐level transcriptome analysis
sec.p: Transcripts encoding miRNAs that were differentially expressed in cases compared to both control groups were identified, 22 , 23 including those that were nutrient‐sensitive, from the DEG list and used to construct miRNA regulatory networks for DEGs in cases.

The Cytoscape plugin iRegulon (version 1.3) was used to identify transcription factors (TFs) predicted to co‐regulate DEGs in cases (compared to PT controls and controls). 24 TFs with nutrient cofactors were also identified and used to construct nutrient‐dependent TF‐DEG regulatory networks. 19

sec.title: Exploratory subgroup analysis of placental transcriptome profiles in cases with poor growth
sec.p: Subgroup analysis was done to explore gene expression signatures in the placenta that may associate with poor fetal growth in cases. The cases who had both a low birthweight (LBW; <2500 g), and birthweight percentile less than 40th for GA at delivery, were classified as LBW cases (n = 6). 25 , 26 Five cases with normal birth weight (NBW; ≥2500 g) or birthweights greater than or equal to 40th percentile were classified as NBW cases. Gene‐, pathway‐, and regulatory network‐level analyses were repeated for LBW cases (n = 6) versus PT controls and controls (n = 21), and NBW cases (n = 5) versus PT controls and controls (n = 21), to identify placental transcriptomic signatures that were unique to cases with suboptimal growth outcomes.

sec.title: Microarray data visualizations
sec.p: DEGs were visualized in volcano plots (VolcaNoseR2 27 ) and heatmaps (Heatmapper, 28 JMP [version 16.0; SAS Institute Inc.]). Cytoscape (version 3.8.2) was used to construct GSEA enrichment maps, nutrient‐gene interaction networks, and TF‐ and miRNA‐DEG regulatory networks. 21 , 29

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data were analyzed using JMP (version 16.0; SAS Institute). Associations between study group (PT controls, controls, and cases) and maternal/infant outcomes were tested using one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA; parametric data) and the Wilcoxon Rank Sum test (nonparametric). Differences in infant outcomes between groups were also assessed in adjusted analyses: linear models/Tukey's HSD for continuous variables and nominal logistic regression models/Likelihood Ratio Chi Square test for categorical variables. Adjusted models included infant sex (male and female) and gestational age at delivery (20–41 weeks). Significance was set at p < 0.05.

We assessed associations between maternal dietary recall data and DEGs using Spearman's rank correlation test (ρ with raw and false discovery rate [FDR]‐adjusted p values [q‐value]) and principal components analysis. Continuous data are reported as median (interquartile range) with p values from ANOVA/Wilcoxon (unadjusted) and multiple linear regression models (adjusted), and categorical data are n (%) with p values from Likelihood Ratio Chi Square. Significance was set at q < 0.05.

sec.title: Clinical cohort characteristics
sec.p: As expected from the study design, all three groups were highly similar (Table 1). Six cases underwent in utero fetal SB closure and six case pregnancies (50%) underwent labor induction for pregnancy termination (Table 2). PT controls were more likely than controls and cases to be male sex. There were no differences in GA at delivery between cases and PT controls, however, both groups had a shorter average gestation length than controls.

sec.title: Case placentae have dysregulated gene expression compared to PT controls and controls
sec.p: One SB control sample failed RNA quality checks, leading to the following final sample sizes for transcriptome sequencing: PT controls (n = 12), controls (n = 9), and cases (n = 12). In a comparison of global placental gene expression profiles, 1705 annotated DEGs were identified in cases compared to PT controls (downregulated: n = 779 and upregulated: n = 926), and 726 were identified in cases compared to controls (downregulated: n = 388 and upregulated: n = 338; Figure S1). The overlap between these two gene lists was identified and carried forward for further analyses (n = 391 DEGs: downregulated: n = 213, upregulated: n = 178; Figure S2).

The top protein classes for downregulated genes in cases were transporters, protein modifying enzymes, and defense/immunity proteins, whereas the top protein classes for upregulated genes were gene‐specific transcriptional regulators, protein modifying enzymes, and metabolite interconversion enzymes (Figure S3). The full lists of DEGs are provided in Tables S2–S4.

sec.title: Cases have downregulation in genes known to be enriched in placental stromal cells and upregulation in genes with known trophoblastic expression
sec.p: Of the 391 annotated DEGs in cases, 110 (28.1%) had known cell‐specific expression at the maternal‐fetal interface, of which, 69 (17.6%) had known cell‐specific expression in placental tissues. In general, we observed upregulation in genes with known placental cell‐specific expression within the placental villi (Hofbauer cells and fetal fibroblasts), and downregulation in genes with known expression in plasma membrane cells (villous cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast, and extra villous cytotrophoblast; Figure 1).

caption.p: Differentially expressed genes in cases (vs. PT controls and controls) have known cell‐specific enrichment in placental tissues. Heat maps show average expression for each study group (columns 1–3; left to right) and mean fold change expression in cases (vs. PT controls and controls; column 4) for genes with known cell‐specific expression in trophoblast (top row of heat maps) and stromal cells (bottom row of heat maps). Placental‐cell specific enrichment was evident for 69 (17.6%) DEGs in cases. Placental cell‐specific expression was determined using PlacentalCellEnrich (dataset: Vento‐Tormo R et al.). Avg, average; C1, cluster 1; C2, cluster 2; controls, full term controls; DEGs, differentially expressed genes; PT controls, preterm controls.

sec.p: Downregulated genes in cases with known expression in placental trophoblasts included solute carrier family 39 member 8 (SLC39A8; transporter of essential metals), riboflavin kinase (RFK; enzyme involved in riboflavin [vitamin B2] utilization), and Ferredoxin 1 (FDX1; involved in vitamin D metabolism). Placental growth factor (PlGF), a pro‐angiogenic regulator of placental vasculogenesis and non‐branching angiogenesis, was also downregulated in cases and has known trophoblastic expression.

Upregulated genes in cases with known expression in Hofbauer cells included hematopoietic Prostaglandin D Synthase (HPGDS; involved in inflammatory response regulation), whereas genes with known expression in fibroblasts included extracellular matrix structural proteins and growth factors.

sec.title: Case placentae have downregulated nutrient transport and upregulated immune and inflammatory processes and branching angiogenesis
sec.p: GSEA revealed 437 dysregulated gene sets in cases compared to PT controls (downregulated: n = 124 and upregulated: n = 313), and 528 dysregulated gene sets in cases compared to controls (downregulated: n = 306 and upregulated: n = 222; Tables S5 and S6). There were 122 dysregulated gene sets in cases compared both PT controls and controls (downregulated: n = 30 and upregulated: n = 92; Figure 2a and Table S7).

caption.p: Differentially expressed gene sets and transcription factors and miRNAs co‐regulating differentially expressed genes in case placentae. (a) Geneset enrichment analysis revealed 122 dysregulated gene sets (nodes) in cases compared to PT controls and controls (downregulated in cases: n = 30 [blue nodes], upregulated in cases: n = 92 [pink nodes]). (b) Seventy‐eight TFs (diamonds) putatively regulating 209 (53.3%) DEGs in cases. TFs are loosely grouped according to module (i.e., sets of TFs targeting the same or a similar subset of DEGs). (c) Four differentially expressed miRNAs in cases (diamonds) are known to target 10 DEGs (2.6%) in cases. ABC, ATP‐binding cassette; COPII, Coat protein complex II; DEGs, differentially expressed genes; ECM, extracellular matrix; ER, endoplasmic reticulum; FC, fold change; GSE, gene set enrichment; PT, preterm; SLC, Solute carrier; SHP2, SH2 containing protein tyrosine phosphatase‐2; TF, transcription factor.

sec.p: Downregulated gene sets in cases included coat protein complex II (COPII)‐mediated vesicle transport from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the Golgi apparatus, ER organization and signaling, protein localization (within the ER and to the cell membrane), and glycosylation. Gene sets involved in transmembrane influx and efflux transport, including solute carrier (SLC) transport (amino acid transport) and ATP‐binding cassette (ABC) transport, and lipid metabolism, were also downregulated.

Upregulated gene sets included immune and inflammatory processes (interleukin 6‐mediated signaling events, positive regulation of chemokine production and activated T cell proliferation, and the inflammatory response pathway) and spinal cord injury, and the largest, and most interconnected cluster of upregulated pathways in cases were involved in translation and protein synthesis. Cases also had upregulation in O‐linked glycosylation‐related pathways, including O‐glycosylation of TSR domain‐containing proteins, and defective beta‐1,3‐glucosyltransferase (B3GALTL) causes Peters plus syndrome (associates with delayed growth and neurodevelopment and cleft lip/palate). Gene sets involved in branching angiogenesis, extracellular matrix formation (namely collagen formation), organization, and signaling, as well as the Hedgehog and Wnt signaling pathways (critical regulators of cell proliferation, differentiation, and development) were also upregulated in cases.

sec.title: Differentially expressed genes in case placentae have common transcriptional regulators
sec.p: At the gene regulatory network level, we identified 78 unique TFs, associated with 59 DNA motifs/tracks, putatively regulating 209 (53.3%) DEGs in cases (Figure 2b, Table S8). The top candidate TFs (i.e., those associated with the most enriched DNA motifs/tracks in the DEG list) were TROVE domain family, member 2 (TROVE2; regulating 14.1% of DEGs [n = 55] in cases), heat shock transcription factors (HSF1, HSF2, and HSF4; regulating 6.7% of DEGs [n = 26] in cases), zinc finger protein 207 (ZNF207; regulating 5.4% of DEGs [n = 21] in cases), DEAD‐Box helicase 4 (DDX4; regulating 19.9% of DEGs [n = 78] in cases), and high mobility group AT‐hook 1 (HMGA1; regulating 11.5% of DEGs [n = 45] in cases). Pleckstrin Homology Like Domain Family A Member 2 (PHLDA2) was predicted to target the largest proportion of DEGs in cases (n = 124 [31.7%]).

Two of the TFs predicted to regulate DEGs were upregulated in cases (transcription factor 4 [TCF4]: mean FC = 2.1, mean q = 0.01; and catalase [CAT]: mean FC = 2.4, mean q = 0.01). TCF4 and CAT were both upregulated in cases in the gene‐level transcriptome analysis and were predicted to regulate 6.7% (n = 26) and 20.4% (n = 80) of DEGs in cases, respectively. No other TFs predicted to regulate DEGs in cases were dysregulated.

We also identified nine miRNAs that were differentially expressed in cases in the gene‐level transcriptome analysis (Table S4). Collectively, these differentially expressed miRNAs targeted 10 DEGs (2.6%) in cases, however, only two of these DEG targets were among the top 50 dysregulated genes in cases (solute carrier family 7, member 1 [SLC7A1]: mean FC in cases = −5.8, q = 0.02; collagen, type V, alpha 1 [COL5A1]: mean FC in cases = 4.6, q = 0.003).

sec.title: Nutrient‐sensitive genes and gene networks are dysregulated in case placentae
sec.p: To determine the extent to which DEGs in cases were nutrient‐dependent, and with which nutrients DEGs interact, we identified 42 DEGs (10.7%) in cases that coded for a protein with a nutrient cofactor (downregulated: n = 19 and upregulated: n = 23). Nutrient cofactors included: calcium (for n = 12 genes), B vitamins (n = 7), iron/heme (n = 6), and zinc (n = 11; Figure 3a).

caption.p: Differentially expressed genes in cases compared to PT controls and controls have nutrient cofactors (a) and are co‐regulated by nutrient‐sensitive TFs (b) and differentially expressed miRNAs (c). (a) DEGs in cases (circular nodes) that code for nutrient (cofactor; diamonds) ‐dependent proteins. DEGs are colored and clustered by their nutrient cofactors (diamonds). The colors used for each micronutrient and linked DEGs were chosen arbitrarily. DEGs with more than one nutrient cofactor are colored gray. Data on nutrient‐gene (protein) interactions were obtained from Scott‐Boyer et al. (2016). (b) Nutrient‐dependent TFs predicted to regulate DNA motifs or tracks enriched in DEGs. TFs (gray diamonds) are linked to their nutrient cofactors (colored diamonds) in the network. (c) One differentially expressed miRNA (gray diamond) in cases is known to target DEGs, and is sensitive to zinc, calcium, and magnesium activity (colored diamonds). In panels b and c, DEGs are circle nodes, with increased (pink) or decreased (blue) expression in cases compared to PT controls and controls. DEGs, differentially expressed genes; FC, fold change; PT, preterm; TF, transcription factor.

sec.p: Next, we identified nutrient‐sensitive regulators (TFs and miRNAs) that target DEGs in cases, to determine which nutrients the gene networks dysregulated in cases were sensitive to. Of the TFs predicted to target DEGs, five (6.4%) had nutrient cofactors (Figure 3b). These included C‐terminal binding protein 2 (CTBP2; vitamin B3‐dependent), CAT (vitamin B3‐, manganese‐, and heme‐dependent), TROVE2 (metal cation‐dependent), adenosine deaminase RNA specific B1 (ADARB1; IP‐6‐ and zinc‐dependent), and E1A binding protein P300 (EP300; zinc‐ and vitamin B5‐dependent). Collectively, these nutrient‐dependent TFs were predicted to target 45.9% of DEGs in cases (heme‐dependent: 20.4% of DEGs, manganese: 20.4% of DEGs, metal cation: 14.0% of DEGs, IP‐6: 17.6% of DEG, vitamin B3: 35.2% of DEGs, vitamin B5: 23.2% of DEGs; zinc: 31.9% of DEGs). One of the downregulated miRNAs in cases (MIR4728) was known to be sensitive to zinc, calcium, and magnesium activity (Figure 3c).

sec.title: Cases with poor growth and low birthweight have unique placental transcriptome profiles
sec.p: Compared to all PT controls and controls, global placental gene expression profiles differed more in LBW cases (n = 213 annotated DEGs; downregulated in LBW cases: n = 148, upregulated in LBW cases: n = 65; Table S9) than NBW cases (n = 18 annotated DEGs, all upregulated in NBW cases; Table S10). To characterize gene signatures unique to LBW cases, we focused on DEGs and dysregulated gene sets that were unique to LBW cases (Figure 4a,b; Table S11).

caption.p: Differentially expressed placental genes, gene sets, and gene networks unique to cases with suboptimal growth. (a) Volcano plot of genes with increased (n = 60) and decreased (n = 148) expression in LBW cases only compared to PT controls and controls. Differential expression was determined at absolute FC greater than or equal to 2.0 and FDR p value (q) less than 0.05. (b) Gene set enrichment analysis revealed 154 dysregulated gene sets (nodes) in LBW cases only, compared to PT controls and controls (downregulated in LBW cases: n = 125 [blue nodes], upregulated in LBW cases: n = 29 [pink nodes]). (c) Forty‐two TFs putatively regulating enriched DNA motifs associated with 131 (63%) DEGs unique to LBW cases were identified. Top enriched TFs (diamonds; normalized enrichment score >3) are visualized. (d) Twenty‐six (12.5%) of DEGs in LBW cases (circular nodes) code for proteins that are nutrient dependent (cofactors; diamonds). DEGs are colored and clustered by their nutrient cofactors. DEGs with more than one nutrient cofactor are colored gray. (e) Nutrient‐dependent enriched TFs predicted to regulate DNA motifs or tracks enriched in DEGs in LBW cases. TFs are linked to their nutrient cofactors (colored diamonds) in the network. Edges (lines) connecting nodes (circles/diamonds in b–e) indicate gene set interactions (b), TF‐regulatory target links (c, e), or nutrient‐gene interactions (d). Controls, full term controls; DEG, differentially expressed genes; FC, fold change; FDR, false discovery rate; GSE, gene set enrichment; LBW, low birth weight; PT controls, preterm controls; TF, transcription factor.

sec.p: The top protein classes for genes downregulated in LBW cases only were protein modifying enzymes and transporters, whereas the top protein classes for genes upregulated in LBW cases were metabolite interconversion enzymes, protein modifying enzymes, and gene‐specific transcriptional regulators (Table S12).

At the pathway level, LBW case placentae had dysregulation in 154 unique gene sets compared to PT controls and controls (downregulated: n = 125, upregulated: n = 29; Figure 4b). LBW cases had downregulation in gene sets involved in COPII‐mediated vesicle transport from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, ER organization and signaling, protein localization (within the ER and to the cell membrane), and glycosylation (Figure 4b, Table S13). LBW cases also had downregulated amino acid transport, transmembrane (ABC) transport, and lipid metabolism (Figure 4b, Table S13). Conversely, whereas NBW cases also had downregulation in pathways related to COPII‐mediated vesicle transport, protein localization, and amino acid transport, they were fewer in number than the changes seen in these pathways in LBW cases (15 pathways total in NBW cases vs. 56 pathways in LBW cases; Tables S13, 14). NBW cases did not have downregulation in lipid metabolism and transmembrane (ABC) transport, as seen in LBW cases. LBW cases had upregulation in gene sets related to protein synthesis (n = 27 pathways) and one apoptosis‐related pathway (Figure 4b, Tables S13 and 14).

At the gene regulatory network level, we identified 42 TFs putatively regulating enriched DNA motifs that associated with 131 (63%) DEGs unique to LBW cases (Table S15). Seven TFs were significantly enriched, predicted to collectively regulate 127 (61.1%) DEGs unique to LBW cases (Figure 4c). The most enriched candidate TFs was interferon regulatory factor 4 (IRF4; regulating 10.6% of DEGs [n = 22] unique to LBW cases; Table S15).
Although there were four miRNAs that were differentially expressed in LBW cases, and not NBW cases, compared to PT controls and controls (Table S11), none were known to target DEGs in LBW cases.

There were 26 DEGs (12.5%) unique to LBW cases that coded for a protein with a nutrient cofactor (Figure 4d). Notably, the B vitamin‐interacting genes that were dysregulated in LBW cases included genes involved in the metabolism of B vitamins (downregulated: riboflavin kinase [RFK; vitamin B2], alkaline phosphatase, placental [ALPP] and placental like 2 [ALPPL2; vitamin B6]); upregulated: thiamin pyrophosphokinase 1 [TPK1; vitamin B1]).

There were two enriched TFs that had nutrient cofactors and targeted DEGs unique to LBW cases (Figure 4e): exonuclease 5 (EXO5; iron‐ and magnesium‐dependent with a known role in DNA repair) and EP300 (vitamin B5‐ and zinc‐dependent with known roles in a transcription factor with known roles in cell growth, differentiation, and NTDs). Collectively, these two nutrient‐dependent TFs were predicted to target 24.5% of DEGs unique to LBW cases (Figure 4e).

sec.title: Maternal nutrient intakes are poorer in case pregnancies compared to controls
sec.p: In 24‐hour dietary recalls, mothers of cases reported lower intakes of choline, potassium, and vitamins A, B6, B12, C, and D than controls (Table S16). Case mothers also met a lower overall proportion of estimated average requirements (EARs) than controls (55.3% [50, 67.1] vs. 81.6% [67.1, 84.2] EARs met, p = 0.01; Figure 5a).

caption.p: Maternal dietary intakes and differential placental gene expression patterns in cases and controls. (a) Mothers of cases met a lower proportion of nutrient EARs (i.e., fell in a lower quartile for % EARs met) than those of controls (p = 0.006). (b) There were no differences between cases and controls for overall HEI score rating. (c) Mothers of cases had higher DII scores (i.e., fell in a higher quartile for DII score) than those of controls (p = 0.04). (d–f) Principal component analysis of cases (diamonds) and controls (circles) based on the 391 differentially expressed genes in cases versus PT controls and controls, with data representing the (d) quartile of overall % EARs met, (e) HEI score rating, and (f) DII score quartile overlayed in coloring to visualize relationships between dietary recall data and differential gene expression patterns. Width of mosaic plots (a–c) = proportional to group size. Q, quartile. DII, Dietary Inflammatory Index; EARs, estimated average requirements; HEI, Health Eating Index.

sec.p: Mothers of cases also had lower scores for adequacy of total fruit and vegetable intakes and intake of refined grains in moderation, and higher overall Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) scores compared to controls (Figure 5b,c, Table S17).

No associations between maternal dietary intake variables and DEGs persisted after FDR‐correction (Table S18). Although there was loose clustering of cases whose mothers met 54–62% of their overall proportion of nutrient EARs, and among controls with the lowest quartile of maternal DII score, no clear separation between study participants was evident based on key dietary recall data and differential gene expression (Figure 5d–e).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Here, we identified multiple novel genes and gene regulatory networks, including those that are nutrient‐sensitive, that were dysregulated in placentae of fetuses with isolated SB. Our work uncovered four major themes related to placental dysfunction in fetuses with isolated SB, advancing our understanding of SB phenotypes and placental mechanisms that may contribute to comorbidities in affected fetuses. First, we found dysregulation in gene networks that have known links to NTDs, but which have not been previously profiled in the placenta. Second, we identified new signatures in fundamental placental processes, including placental transport and growth, that were dysregulated in cases. Next, we found that several of the dysregulated placental gene networks in cases were sensitive to multiple nutrients, and that mothers of cases reported dietary intakes with lower nutritional value and higher inflammatory potential. These findings support a need to expand beyond a folic acid‐centric view to understand NTD phenotypes and comorbidities. Last, we found dysregulation in gene networks related to inflammation and immune regulation in cases. Collectively, our findings suggest that the placental transcriptome is altered in fetuses with SB, and that placental dysfunction in fetuses with SB may, in part, underlie poor fetal growth, and contribute to subsequent comorbidities 30 and increased risk of mortality. 31

We have shown that several genes and gene sets with known links to NTDs are dysregulated in placentae from fetuses with isolated SB. The COPII pathway was downregulated in case placentae and is a critical regulator of forward trafficking of proteins and lipids from the ER. 32 Disruptions in COPII‐mediated vesicular ER‐to‐Golgi transport have been linked to SB via the transporting role of COPII. 33 Wnt and Hedgehog pathways have been associated with NTDs through their regulatory role in neural tube closure 34 , 35 and were both upregulated in case placentae. Notably, cases also had downregulation in gene sets involved in glycosylation and upregulation in protein synthesis, which could be compensatory for reductions in COPII‐mediated ER‐to‐Golgi protein transport. Last, CAT was upregulated in case placentae and identified as a putative transcriptional regulator of 20% of DEGs. CAT responds to oxidative stress within the cell, including ER stress that can arise due to protein accumulation, 36 and maternal CAT functional capacity may be altered in pregnancies with fetal NTDs. 37 Collectively, these findings suggest that gene expression signatures associated with NTDs may be identifiable in placentae from affected pregnancies, and that studying placentae from fetuses with NTDs could provide novel insights into NTD phenotypes.

Cases also had dysregulation in placental gene networks related to placental growth, which could contribute to placental dysfunction and common SB‐associated comorbidities, such as poor fetal growth. Specifically, cases had upregulation in gene sets related to placental branching angiogenesis, and genes known to be expressed by Hofbauer cells and fibroblasts, which both play critical roles in placental angiogenesis. 38 , 39 Two insulin like growth factor family genes, which have been associated with accelerated placental villous maturity, 40 were also upregulated in cases. Conversely, cases had decreased expression of two pro‐angiogenic genes: PlGF (involved in non‐branching angiogenesis 41 ) and Erb‐B2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinase 2 (ERBB2; involved in trophoblast migration and differentiation 42 ). Collectively, these signaling alterations may have led to premature villous differentiation toward terminal villi, 43 , 44 which can diminish the placenta's capacity to grow and lead to placental dysfunction. 45 , 46 These transcriptomic signatures may also suggest a placental phenotype in cases that is consistent with findings in our previous work with a historical cohort, where isolated fetal NTDs associated with increased placental Hofbauer cell levels and increased risk of placental villous hypermaturity. 7 Altogether, our findings indicate that cases have altered activity in placental angiogenic genes and gene sets, which may place them at an increased risk of placental villous maldevelopment and subsequent fetal comorbidities.

Cases also had general downregulation of genes known to be enriched in villous trophoblast cells, ABC transport pathways (essential for placental efflux and the transport of nutrients and inflammatory molecules), and SLC transport genes and pathways, which influx a wide range of nutritional and exogenous compounds. 47 More of these pathways were downregulated in cases with LBW compared to controls, rather than cases with NBW, suggesting that a potential compromise in placental barrier and nutrient transport function may underly poor growth in fetuses with SB, increasing risk of subsequent morbidities. Future studies of larger cohorts should robustly explore placental gene expression in fetuses with SB and suboptimal growth.

Whereas maternal folate status has been the primary nutrient target for NTD prevention to‐date, we found that cases had dysregulation in placental gene networks sensitive to nutrients beyond folate, including other B vitamins, zinc, calcium, inositol, and metals/metal cations. As folate deficiency is rare in the folic acid‐fortified Canadian population, 48 NTD risk may be, in part, attributable to low bioavailability of other nutritional factors; namely, one carbon metabolism cofactors (vitamins B6, B12, and choline). 49 In Canada, vitamin B12 deficiency has been identified in ~5% of adults 48 and may affect nearly one in five pregnant women in early pregnancy, 50 whereas vitamin B6 deficiency may affect around 10% of women of child bearing age. 51 Here, mothers of cases reported lower absolute intakes in vitamins B6, B12, and choline, but not folate, as well as vitamins C and D, and overall, met a lower proportion of their estimated nutrient requirements. 52 , 53 Further, nearly half of DEGs in cases were putatively co‐regulated by TFs dependent on nutrients with known links to NTDs, including zinc 1 and inositol, 54 and four of the five nutrient‐dependent TFs (CAT, CTBPR2, TROVE2, and EP300) predicted to regulate DEGs in cases were also identified as top TFs targeting DEGs in fetuses with NTDs in our previous study. 20 Nutrient cofactors for these TFs included zinc, vitamins B3 and B5, inositol hexaphosphate, and heme. As the placenta is a rapidly developing and metabolically active organ, with considerable nutritional requirements itself throughout gestation, low bioavailability of these nutrients may be not only permissive of fetal NTDs, but also placental maldevelopment and dysfunction in nutrient‐sensitive gene networks, increasing risk subsequent offspring morbidities.

We have also shown that placentae from fetuses with isolated SB have increased expression in immune and inflammatory processes, which could increase risk of poor fetal outcomes. 55 Specifically, cases had upregulation in immune and inflammatory process gene sets, and in genes with known expression in Hofbauer cells. As well, ZNF207, which was predicted to target one of the most enriched DNA modules in DEGs in cases overall, and IRF4 and transcription factor 7 (TCF7), two enriched TFs targeting DEGs in LBW cases specifically, all have known roles in transcriptional regulation of immune development and response. 56 , 57 Maternal immune dysregulation and increased inflammatory load are known to associate with increased risk of fetal NTDs, 2 and, here, mothers of cases also reported dietary intakes with higher dietary inflammatory potential than controls. 58 Further, following failed closure of the neural tube, “secondary lesion cascades,” activated in response to spinal cord injury, may induce ongoing pro‐inflammatory molecular and cellular signaling alterations. 59 In this study, case placentae also had increased expression in gene sets responding to spinal cord injury. Altogether, our findings suggest that placental inflammatory processes may be elevated in case pregnancies, with possible contributions from NTD‐related biological processes and/or maternal dietary inflammatory potential. As placental inflammation is known to increase risk of fetal morbidity and mortality, understanding whether inflammatory load is heightened in placentae from fetuses with NTDs should be a focus of further study.

Our ability to draw conclusions about the dietary recall data presented in this study are limited by the fact that only a single recall was collected, that it is known that participants often under‐report dietary intakes, and an objective assessment of nutritional biomarkers to validate recall results was not available. Half of the cases were also delivered following pregnancy termination, however, as terminations occurred at an earlier GA than the liveborn cases delivered, it is difficult to delineate the potential effects of the termination procedure versus GA on placental gene expression. This is a limitation of our study, and a larger cohort would be needed to evaluate the effects of termination or liveborn with fetoscopic repair on placental phenotype in fetuses with SB. Further, whereas the inclusion of an additional control group (PT controls) that was GA‐matched to cases is a strength of this study, placental dysfunction is associated with PT birth, and it is possible that the PT controls themselves may have had placental maldevelopment, which could have confounded our comparisons. However, in an aim to address this limitation, we took a conservative approach when identifying the DEG list, and only considered the overlap between the two comparison lists: cases compared to controls (who were born full term) and cases compared to PT controls. Last, our finding that DEGs in cases had known cell‐specific expression in placental tissues relied on a single‐cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‐Seq) dataset generated using first trimester placental samples. 18 Future studies should consider referencing placental scRNA‐Seq datasets generated from later gestational timepoints to determine whether these findings are replicated, given that cases were delivered in both the second and third trimesters.

This is the first study to assess global placental gene expression in fetuses with isolated SB, and among the first to interrogate placental phenotype in pregnancies with fetal NTDs more broadly. Our findings increase our understanding of placental function in pregnancies with isolated fetal SB, and report multiple novel gene regulatory networks, including those that are sensitive to nutrient activity and levels, that may associate with SB phenotype and comorbidities. Our findings of dysregulated gene networks known to associate with SB pathogenesis suggests functional perturbations contributing to SB may also present in placentae, which could contribute to placental dysfunction. Studying placental maldevelopment and dysfunction, including nutrient‐gene interactions, in fetuses with isolated SB may help identify novel mechanisms associated with comorbidities in fetuses with SB and new targets for improving fetal outcomes.
